passage: The temple fair in Wadgaon was too bright and too loud, and Jaya had not slept since morning. When her red balloon slipped from her fist, she screamed and dropped flat onto the dust, kicking. People turned to stare. Tushar crouched beside her. "The nap went missing today, na?" No scolding. He lifted her, found the shade behind the bangle stall, and rocked her with her cheek on his shoulder. Soon her fists opened, and she was asleep.

qa.q: What slipped from Jaya's fist?
qa.a: Her red balloon slipped from her fist.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling when she dropped onto the dust?
qa.a: She was overwhelmed and angry; with no sleep since morning, losing the balloon was more than she could cope with.

qa.q: What did Tushar do that helped?
qa.a: He stayed calm, did not scold, and carried her to a quiet shady spot to rock her, which let her tired body finally sleep.

qa.q: How might the people staring read Jaya's screaming?
qa.a: They might see a naughty child, when really she was a tired toddler whose coping had run out.

grounding: Shows a toddler who missed her nap collapsing over a small loss because her tired brain has no coping left.

passage: Diego had spent his nap time in the car seat, wide awake, on the long drive back to Gothenburg. At the supermarket, Astrid handed him a banana, and it snapped in half. Diego howled as if the world had ended, then wrapped himself around her leg and would not let go. Astrid looked at the half-full cart, then at his red, wet face. She parked the cart beside the bread, carried him out to the car, and drove home. He was asleep before the second traffic light.

qa.q: Where did Diego spend his nap time?
qa.a: In the car seat, wide awake, on the long drive back to Gothenburg.

qa.q: Why did Diego howl when the banana snapped?
qa.a: He was so tired that a tiny disappointment felt huge and upsetting; he had no calm left to cope with it.

qa.q: Which choice of Astrid's worked, and why?
qa.a: Leaving the half-full cart and taking him home to sleep, because rest, not a lecture, was what his body needed.

qa.q: What might it be like for Astrid to leave the shopping behind?
qa.a: It may feel frustrating to abandon the half-full cart, but she put Diego's rest ahead of finishing the task.

grounding: Shows a toddler who missed a nap falling apart and clinging over a small upset, and a caregiver treating it as tiredness rather than naughtiness.

passage:
Monday: Guests came, and Manoj skipped his nap. By four he was screaming on the floor because his milk was in the green cup, not the blue one.
Tuesday: A wedding band played outside. No nap. He bit his sister's hand over a crayon, then sobbed into Noor's dupatta.
Thursday: Noor shut the windows, drew the curtain, and lay beside him at one. He slept two hours. At four he drank from the green cup without a word.

qa.q: What cup was Manoj's milk in on Monday?
qa.a: His milk was in the green cup, not the blue one.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling when he sobbed into Noor's dupatta on Tuesday?

qa.q: What changed on Thursday, and why did it help?
qa.a: Noor made the room dark and quiet and lay beside him at one, so he got his nap and could cope with the green cup at four.

qa.q: How might Manoj's sister see the crayon fight?
qa.a: She was hurt and might think Manoj was just being mean, not knowing tiredness had used up his patience.

grounding: Shows a toddler's missed naps turning small frustrations into screaming, biting and sobbing, and a protected nap restoring his coping.

subtype: Sleepy child rubbing eyes and getting wild [Observer]

subtype: Sleepy child rubbing eyes and getting wild [Observer]
passage: At the Kothrud daycare, Wasim was zooming between the cots at two o'clock, laughing so loudly that the helper frowned. "That one is being naughty again," she said. Rajni watched a little longer. His eyes were pink, and between laps he kept rubbing them with his fists. When he tripped on a cushion, the laughter turned into wailing in a second. Rajni picked him up and carried him to the corner mat under the slow fan. "Not naughty. Sleepy," she told the helper. He was snoring before she finished humming.

qa.q: What time was Wasim zooming between the cots?
qa.a: At two o'clock.

qa.q: What made Rajni look past the helper's view?

qa.a: The helper sees a naughty child being loud, missing that he is overtired and needs his nap.

passage:
Week one: Every night was a fight. Kalyani bargained, "One more cartoon, then sleep?" and scolded when Varun ran off. He cried until eleven.
Week two: She tried something new. A warm bath at eight, the big light off and the lamp on, the same lullaby about the moon, the same long cuddle with his blue blanket. He fussed, but less.
Week four: At the first splash of bathwater, Varun yawned and reached for the blue blanket himself. By the end of the moon song, his eyes were closed.

qa.q: What lullaby did Kalyani sing?
qa.a: The same lullaby about the moon.

qa.q: How does Varun seem to feel about bedtime by week four?
qa.a: He seems calm and safe, yawning at the bathwater and reaching for his blue blanket himself.

qa.q: Why did the new routine work better than bargaining?
qa.a: The same steps every night told Varun what came next, so he felt secure, while bargaining and scolding kept him guessing and upset.

qa.q: What would bedtime be like for Kalyani if she had kept bargaining?
qa.a: She would likely keep facing fights and tears until eleven, ending every night drained and frustrated.

grounding: Shows a predictable wind-down of bath, dim light, song and cuddle replacing bargaining and scolding and helping a toddler settle.

passage: The new flat in Chandigarh still smelled of paint, and two-year-old Gurleen stood in the doorway of the strange bedroom, lip trembling. Charu didn't argue or promise sweets. She did exactly what they did at home: a warm bath with the yellow duck, the ceiling light off and the small lamp on, the Punjabi lullaby Nani used to sing, and the same cuddle, Gurleen's head tucked under her chin. Halfway through the second verse the trembling stopped. Gurleen sighed, patted Charu's cheek twice, and slept in the new room.

qa.q: What toy was in Gurleen's bath?
qa.a: The yellow duck.

qa.q: What does Gurleen's trembling lip in the doorway suggest?
qa.a: She feels scared and unsure in the strange new bedroom.

qa.q: Why did Charu repeat the home routine instead of promising sweets?
qa.a: The familiar bath, lamp, lullaby and cuddle told Gurleen's body that sleep was safe, even in a new place.

qa.q: How might Charu feel as Gurleen pats her cheek and falls asleep?
qa.a: She is probably relieved and tender, glad the first night in the new flat ended calmly.

grounding: Shows the same bath, dim light, song and cuddle telling a toddler that sleep is safe, even in an unfamiliar room.

passage:
"Farida, she won't sleep. I said no park tomorrow unless she closes her eyes."
"Abbu, please don't bargain. Warm bath first, then only the night lamp."
"Then?"

Twenty minutes later the phone buzzed.
"Farida? She's asleep on my shoulder. No threats needed."

passage:
Note for Parul's parents, Saturday night.
Bedtime went fine in the end, but here is how it went. After the story, Parul asked for water. Then a second story. Then she told me her toe hurt. Then she asked, very quietly, whether you were coming back tonight. I think that was the real question. I sat on the edge of her bed and said, "Yes. Mummy and Papa will be here when you wake up. I'm right outside." I left the door open a hand's width. She asked for one more hug, got it, and was asleep in ten minutes.
Farhan

qa.q: How wide did Farhan leave the door open?
qa.a: A hand's width.

qa.q: What was Parul worried about underneath all the requests?
qa.a: She was anxious about whether her parents were coming back tonight; the dark and being apart from them felt big.

qa.q: What did Farhan do that settled Parul?
qa.a: Farhan gave a short, calm answer to the real worry, stayed close by and left the door a little open, instead of scolding the stalling.

qa.q: How might Parul's parents feel reading the note?
qa.a: They might feel touched and reassured that Parul missed them and was comforted gently while they were out.

grounding: Shows a young child's bedtime requests turning out to be a bid for reassurance about being apart, settled by a short, calm answer.

passage: The power went out in Dhanora just after dinner, and the lantern threw big shadows on the mud wall. Varun lay on the charpai beside Hansa Aaji. "Aaji, water." She gave him the steel tumbler. "Aaji, one more story." She told a short one about a clever goat. Then a jackal howled far off, and he sat bolt upright. "Aaji, one more hug?" She pulled him close. "The jackal is in the fields, far away. The door is shut. I'm right here all night." He tucked his cold feet against her legs and was asleep before the lantern flickered.

qa.q: What was Aaji's story about?
qa.a: A clever goat.

qa.q: Why did Varun sit up and ask for one more hug?
qa.a: The jackal's howl in the dark scared him, and he wanted to feel safe and close to Aaji.

qa.q: What made Aaji's answer work?
qa.a: It was short, calm and true: the jackal is far, the door is shut, and she is right there, so he felt reassured without a long argument.

qa.q: How might Aaji see Varun's many requests?
qa.a: She seems to see them as a need for comfort rather than naughtiness, since she answers each one gently.

grounding: Shows a young child's requests for water, stories and hugs as a bid for reassurance in the dark, settled by short calm answers.

passage: It was Freya's first week in her own room in the Dublin house, and every night the list grew. A glass of water. A second glass. The window checked. "Daddy, is the wardrobe closed properly?" Emeka checked it. Tonight she added, "Can you tell me again where you'll be?" He knelt by her bed. "Downstairs, reading. Then in my room, right next to yours. The wall between us is very thin." He knocked on it twice, softly. "That means I'm here." Freya knocked back twice, giggled, and pulled the duvet up to her chin.

qa.q: How many times did Emeka knock on the wall?
qa.a: He knocked on it twice, softly.

qa.q: What was Freya really worried about beneath all the requests?
qa.a: She felt nervous alone in the new room at night and wanted to be reassured that Daddy was close.

qa.q: Why did the knocking idea help?
qa.a: It gave her a short, calm and simple sign that her dad was near, turning the fear into a small game.

qa.q: What might it be like for Emeka to answer the growing list each night?
qa.a: It could feel tiring, but he treats the requests as her need for comfort and stays patient.

grounding: Shows a young child stalling at bedtime because separation feels big at night, and a parent settling it with a short, calm reassurance.

subtype: Parents worn down by broken nights [Receiver]
passage:
Monday: Vaibhav woke three times with bad dreams. At breakfast he spilled his milk, and Mumma shouted, "Can't you do one thing properly?" His lip wobbled. Later Vinita hugged him and said sorry, her eyes red.
Wednesday: Another broken night. Vaibhav tiptoed around the kitchen, quiet as a mouse, watching his mother's face.
Saturday: Papa took the night shift and let Mumma sleep till ten. When Vaibhav knocked over the juice, she only laughed and handed him a cloth. "Mumma's batteries are full today," she said. He wiped the table, grinning.

qa.q: Who took the night shift on Saturday?
qa.a: Papa took the night shift and let Mumma sleep till ten.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav tiptoe around the kitchen on Wednesday?

qa.q: What helped Vinita stay patient on Saturday?
qa.a: Real rest: Papa took the night and she slept till ten, so a spill no longer felt like too much.

qa.q: How might Vinita have felt after shouting on Monday?

grounding: Shows a child on the receiving end of a sleep-deprived parent's snapping, and real rest restoring the parent's patience.

subtype: Parents worn down by broken nights [Receiver]
passage: The power had been off since midnight, the baby had cried four times, and by seven Chaitanya's eyes felt full of sand. Rukmini, five, held out her school shoe. "Appa, the lace is knotted." "Not now!" he snapped, so loudly that she dropped the shoe. She went and sat under the table with her doll. Amma picked up the shoe. "Go and sleep one hour. I'll ask the school van to wait." Chaitanya lay on the cool terrace floor and slept. When he came down, he crawled under the table. "Sorry, kanna. Appa was very tired, not angry with you." Rukmini handed him the shoe again.

qa.q: Where did Rukmini sit after Appa snapped?
qa.a: She went and sat under the table with her doll.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling when she dropped the shoe?
qa.a: She felt startled and hurt by the loud snap, and hid under the table to feel safe.

qa.q: What helped Chaitanya repair the moment?
qa.a: An hour of real sleep, then crawling under the table to say sorry and explain he was tired, not angry with her.

qa.q: How does Chaitanya see his own snapping once he has slept?
qa.a: He sees it came from exhaustion rather than from Rukmini, and he is sorry enough to apologise at her level.

grounding: Shows a young child hurt by a parent's snapping after broken nights, and a short real rest helping the parent repair it.

subtype: Parents worn down by broken nights [Receiver]
passage: Indu had woken Zubin at one, three and five, each time with the same dream about the lift getting stuck. That afternoon in their Dadar flat, she held up a drawing. "Pappa, look, it's you!" "Indu, I'm on a call, stop pestering!" Her face crumpled. Zubin ended the call, knelt, and looked properly: a man with huge eyebrows and a smile. "I'm sorry. I'm so tired my brain is broken." That evening he asked Indu's Nani to keep Indu on Saturday night so he could sleep. Indu packed her own toothbrush, delighted.

qa.q: What was Indu's dream about?
qa.a: The lift getting stuck.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling when her face crumpled?
qa.a: She felt hurt and pushed away, having wanted to share her drawing and getting a snap instead.

qa.q: What was a wise step Zubin took after apologising?
qa.a: He asked Nani to keep Indu on Saturday night so he could get real sleep, rather than just trying harder.

qa.q: How might Zubin feel after snapping at Indu?
qa.a: He probably feels guilty and foggy, aware that his own sleep debt, not the drawing, caused the snap.

grounding: Shows a child receiving a tired parent's snap after repeated night waking, and the parent seeking real rest instead of relying on willpower.

passage:
"Bhavna, page forty-two. Ma'am said forty-two."

passage: Last month, when my baby sister was new, I hardly slept. She cried at night and I lay awake counting cracks in the ceiling. At school I forgot my maths book three days in a row, and Sir wrote "careless" in my diary. At football I shouted at Uday for one bad pass, and then I cried in the toilets, which I never do. Uday found me there. "Mohit, you're not angry, you're sleepy," he said. That night Mamma let me sleep in Dadi's room, far from the crying. The next day I remembered my book.

qa.q: What did Sir write in the diary?
qa.a: Sir wrote "careless" in the diary.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling in the toilets after football?
qa.a: Mohit felt upset and ashamed, crying after shouting at Uday, because tiredness had made everything too much.

qa.q: What finally helped Mohit remember the book?
qa.a: Sleeping in Dadi's room, far from the crying, so Mohit got real rest instead of just trying harder.

qa.q: How does Uday see Mohit's shouting?
qa.a: Uday sees past the anger to the tiredness and says so kindly instead of staying offended.

grounding: Shows a schoolchild short of sleep forgetting things, snapping and crying, being labelled careless, and recovering once real rest is possible.

passage:
Coach's notes, Wednesday
Nitin dropped two easy catches today and twice forgot where I'd placed him. When I called him over, he argued, then his eyes filled up. Last month he was my sharpest fielder, so I didn't send him to run laps. I asked about his evenings. Tuition till eight, homework till eleven, then his cousin's phone games till past midnight. He said, "I try, Coach, but my head is like fog."
I let him sit out the last drill with water and a banana. I called his father tonight and told him what Nitin said. His father was surprised and said they would move the phone out of the room at night.
Harsha

qa.q: Until what time did Nitin do homework?
qa.a: Homework till eleven.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling when his eyes filled up?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and ashamed, trying hard but unable to focus through the fog in his head.

qa.q: Why was asking about evenings wiser than sending Nitin to run laps?
qa.a: It uncovered the real cause, too little sleep, which laps could not fix, and led to a call home and a change at night.

qa.q: How might Nitin's father feel on getting the call?
qa.a: Surprised and probably concerned, but ready to act by moving the phone out of the room.

grounding: Shows a schoolchild short of sleep becoming foggy, forgetful and argumentative, and a coach looking for the cause instead of punishing effort.

subtype: Teacher noticing yawning and short temper [Observer]
passage: Ishita was usually the first hand up in Pradeep Sir's Class 5 in Indore, full of jokes. This week she sat slumped, snapped at her bench partner over an eraser, and was still staring at a blank page ten minutes after everyone had started. Pradeep felt the old urge to say, "Pay attention or stand outside." Instead, at break, he crouched by her desk. "You seem really tired. How's bedtime been?" Ishita rubbed her eyes. "They're building a flyover next to our building. The drilling goes on all night." Pradeep nodded. He gave her a shorter worksheet for the day, moved her to the quiet seat by the window, and wrote a note home asking whether she could nap in the afternoons until the drilling moved on.

qa.q: What is being built next to Ishita's building?
qa.a: A flyover.

qa.q: What was Pradeep tempted to do, and what made him hold back?
qa.a: He felt a flash of irritation and an urge to send her outside, but he held back because he was puzzled and concerned that his cheerful student had changed so much.

qa.q: Which of Pradeep's steps would help most while the drilling goes on?
qa.a: The note home asking about afternoon naps, because it tackles the missing sleep itself, while the shorter worksheet and quiet seat ease the day.

qa.q: What is school like for Ishita this week?
qa.a: She is exhausted and short-tempered, struggling to start work and snapping at her bench partner, far from her usual cheerful self.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a normally cheerful child slumped and irritable and asking gently about bedtime and noise instead of punishing her.

subtype: Teacher noticing yawning and short temper [Observer]
passage:

subtype: Teacher noticing yawning and short temper [Observer]
passage: Last term I nearly punished Swati for sleeping in my maths class. She was the girl who hummed while doing sums, always first to laugh at my terrible jokes. For a week she yawned, put her head down, and once kicked her chair when I called on her. I had the detention slip half written. Then I remembered my own bad months as a student, and after class I asked her, softly, how she was sleeping. Her family had moved in with relatives, she said, and she slept in the hall, where the TV ran till one. I phoned her mother that evening, and they moved her mattress into the small storeroom. Two weeks later Swati was humming again. I, Ganga, still keep that unfinished detention slip in my drawer.

qa.q: Till what time did the TV run in the hall?
qa.a: Till one.

qa.q: Why does Ganga keep the unfinished detention slip?
qa.a: Ganga seems relieved and a little ashamed at how close that punishment came, and keeps the slip as a reminder to ask first.

qa.q: What made asking gently work better than detention?
qa.a: It uncovered the late TV in the hall, and a call to her mother led to a quieter place for Swati to sleep.

qa.q: What was that week like for Swati?
qa.a: She was exhausted and irritable, too tired to hum or laugh, and possibly worried about being in trouble.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a cheerful child slumped and irritable, and asking about noise at home instead of punishing her for inattention.

passage: Last year I thought I'd just turned into a moody person. My brain switched on at eleven at night, like someone had flipped a light, and my alarm went off at 5:45 for a 7:15 school bus. I snapped at Mumma over toast. I fell asleep in history. One morning, half awake, I cycled straight through the red light at the colony gate, and a scooter missed me by a hand's width. Sunaina saw it and made me promise to tell my parents. That evening I did. We read together about how teenage body clocks drift later, and we made a plan: phone charging in the kitchen at ten, curtains open the moment I wake, a real lie-in on Sundays. I'm still not a morning person. But I'm Preeti again, not a grumpy stranger.

qa.q: What time did the alarm go off?
qa.a: At 5:45, for a 7:15 school bus.

qa.q: How did Preeti feel about the moodiness at the time?
qa.a: Preeti felt confused and a bit ashamed, believing the grumpiness was just who Preeti had become rather than tiredness.

qa.q: What did Preeti and the parents put in the plan?
qa.a: Charging the phone in the kitchen at ten, opening the curtains on waking, and a real Sunday lie-in, which protect sleep instead of fighting the body clock.

qa.q: What might Sunaina have felt watching the near miss?
qa.a: Sunaina was probably frightened for Preeti, which explains the push for a promise to tell the parents that same day.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose later body clock clashes with an early school start, leading to low mood, snapping and a risky choice that are partly sleep debt.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Tuesday
Gargi was sent to me after arguing with her first-period teacher for the third time this month. She sat with her hood up and said, "Everyone thinks I've got an attitude." Mostly, she looks exhausted. She told me she can't fall asleep before midnight however hard she tries, and then her alarm rings at six. She has been getting through the day on cold coffee and snapping at friends by lunch.
I explained that teenage body clocks often run later, so this isn't a flaw in her character, but she still needs a plan. Together we listed three things to try, and I called her mother this afternoon to share them. Check-in again on Friday.

passage: In their Nashik flat the tap water came only from six to seven, and every morning Jatin needed Nilesh up to fill the drums. "Nilesh! Six o'clock! Get up!" A grunt. At 6:20 Jatin banged on the door. "Useless boy!" Nilesh stumbled out, filled one drum in silence, and slammed the bathroom door so hard a bucket toppled. That night, after a colleague mentioned how teenagers' sleep runs late, Jatin knocked softly. "Can we make a deal? You're up at 6:15, and no shouting from me. Your phone goes to the hall at 10:30." Nilesh looked at him for a long second. "And no 'useless'?" "No 'useless'." The next morning at 6:15, Nilesh was at the tap, yawning, but talking.

qa.q: When did the tap water come?
qa.a: From six to seven.

qa.q: What does Nilesh's question, "And no 'useless'?", reveal?
qa.a: He had been hurt by the word more than by being woken, and he wanted to feel respected as part of the deal.

qa.q: Why did the deal work better than banging on the door?
qa.a: It set a steady wake time and a phone cut-off both could agree on, and dropping the insult protected their relationship.

qa.q: How does Jatin see the morning fights after talking to his colleague?
qa.a: He begins to see Nilesh's grunts as partly sleepiness rather than laziness, and chooses a deal over shouting.

grounding: Shows a teen on the receiving end of dawn shouting, and a parent who learns about teen sleep and negotiates a phone cut-off and steady wake time.

subtype: Parent fighting with a sleepy teen [Receiver]
passage: Every morning in their Kolkata flat began the same way: Madhuri at Saurabh's door at 5:30, calling his name every two minutes, and Saurabh growling "Five more" into the pillow. On Tuesday he threw his pillow at the door. Madhuri shouted back, and they didn't speak all day. That night she found him at his desk, not studying, just staring. "Why can't you sleep earlier?" she asked, tired now rather than angry. "I try, Ma. My body isn't sleepy till twelve." She thought about that. "Then let's change the plan. You set your own alarm, I stop calling. Screens off at 10:30. Sundays you sleep late." Saurabh blinked. "Seriously?" "Seriously. I'm tired of fighting you." On Wednesday the alarm rang, and he got up on the second snooze. Nobody shouted.

qa.q: What time did Madhuri come to Saurabh's door each morning?
What was Saurabh feeling when he threw his pillow at the door?
qa.a: He felt irritated and cornered, pulled out of sleep by constant calling when his body had not been sleepy until midnight.

qa.q: What made the new plan protect their relationship?
qa.a: It swapped nagging for a fair deal: his own alarm, screens off at 10:30 and Sunday lie-ins, so the dawn fights stopped.

qa.q: How had the mornings affected Madhuri?
qa.a: She was worn out and angry, then simply tired of fighting her son, which opened her to a new plan.

grounding: Shows a teen and parent locked in dawn nagging and slammed responses, and a negotiated plan on screens and wake time easing it.

passage: The night before the chemistry board exam, Imran decided sleep was for the weak. He sat at the desk in his Lucknow flat with three highlighters and a flask of tea until the dawn azaan, flipping through equations. In the exam hall, the first question was one he had highlighted twice. He stared, and his mind was a blank sheet. His palms went wet; his heart thudded. He wrote something, crossed it out, wrote again. At home Bhavna Apa found him with his head on the table. "Ammi says you didn't sleep at all." "I studied everything and remembered nothing." "That's exactly why." Three days later, before physics, he stopped at eleven, slept, and read only his summary sheet over breakfast. His hands still shook, but the answers came.

qa.q: What did Imran read over breakfast before physics?
qa.a: Only his summary sheet.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling when he stared at the first question?
qa.a: He was panicking, palms wet and heart thudding, frightened because his mind went blank on a topic he had studied.

qa.q: What did Imran change before physics, and why did it help?
qa.a: He stopped at eleven and slept, then read just his summary, so his memory and nerves held up better.

qa.q: How might Bhavna feel finding Imran with his head on the table?
qa.a: She is concerned but understanding, and gently points out that skipping sleep caused the blank.

grounding: Shows a student cramming all night, blanking and panicking the next day, then protecting sleep before the next exam.

passage: During my prelims last winter, I believed in one rule: whoever sleeps least wins. I'm Darshan, and I pulled two all-nighters before biology, living on cold tea and fear. By the morning of the paper my eyes burned and the diagrams in my head had turned to soup. At the gate, Irfan asked if I'd revised the kidney chapter, and I bit his head off. Inside, I read the first question and my chest went tight, as if the room had shrunk. I got through, barely. Afterwards Irfan didn't sulk; he just showed me his timetable: study in blocks, stop by eleven, a short recap in the morning. For the finals I copied it. I wasn't magically calm, but I could remember things, and I didn't shout at anyone at the gate.
